entries.topic: Muscadet: Melon alone only in the three named zones
entries.claim: The Loire record calls Melon de Bourgogne Muscadet's only grape and says Muscadet is Melon de Bourgogne alone, and the Régionale question i-r0p7056l says Melon has been the sole grape of Muscadet ever since the winter of 1709.
entries.finding: The specification of the plain Muscadet AOC names Melon B as principal grape and Chardonnay B as an accessory grape, at no more than 10 per cent of a holding's plantings. INAO's standing committee took up the change in 2017, it went to national opposition in November 2018, it stands in the specification homologated by the arrêté of 5 February 2021 (amended 27 May 2021), and the arrêté of 26 November 2025 (JORF of 3 December 2025) keeps it. Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire and Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu remain Melon B alone. The history in the question stands: the specification's link to origin says the hard winter of 1709 destroyed most of the Nantes vineyard and Melon, which bears frost better, was replanted, and InterLoire says the same.

entries.topic: Rueda: one white category since 2019, the main grapes at 75 per cent since 2024
entries.claim: The Rueda and Toro record teaches Rueda Verdejo and Rueda Sauvignon as label categories at 85 per cent of their grape and plain Rueda as at least 50 per cent Verdejo, with Viura merely permitted in that blend; the Spain module question c-lalvjliu and the Verdejo grape fragment repeat the half.
entries.finding: The Consejo Regulador merged Rueda Verdejo, Rueda Sauvignon and Rueda into one white category, Rueda, from the 2019 vintage; the amended pliego (published nationally on 29 October 2019, in force at EU level from 3 March 2020) asked at least 50 per cent of the main whites, then Verdejo and Sauvignon Blanc, and admitted Chardonnay and Viognier as secondary. From 30 August 2024 (BOCYL of that day; EU communication of 12 June 2025) a Rueda white needs at least 75 per cent from the main whites, now Verdejo, Sauvignon Blanc, Viura, Chardonnay and Viognier, and may be all of them. A grape named on the label must still make at least 85 per cent, by EU rule. Plain Rueda therefore has no Verdejo floor of its own. The wines notes for Rueda Verdejo and Rueda Sauvignon and the Verdejo label line say at least 85 per cent of a named grape, which is still true, and are left.

entries.topic: Verdejo and Verdelho: a different grape, not unrelated
entries.claim: The Rueda trap says Verdejo is not Verdelho and that the Madeira grape is unrelated.
entries.finding: They are different varieties, but not shown unrelated: the institutes' catalogue makes Verdejo a probable cross of Savagnin and Castellana Blanca on genetic analyses at Montpellier, and a DNA study of 2018 makes Verdelho an offspring of Savagnin with an unknown other parent, which would make the two half siblings. Both results rest on small marker sets, so the safe wording is a different grape, as the Verdejo and Godello grape fragments already say.

entries.topic: Savagnin: kin to Sauvignon Blanc and Petit Manseng, not only to Gewürztraminer
entries.claim: The Jura record says Savagnin is not Sauvignon Blanc and belongs to the Traminer family, kin to Gewürztraminer (traps[0]), and its vin jaune question calls Sauvignon Blanc a different grape despite the similar name; neither says the two are kin.
entries.finding: True as far as it goes. DNA analyses (reported from 2013) show a parent and offspring tie between Savagnin and Sauvignon Blanc, and Savagnin, recorded far earlier, is taken as the likely parent; analyses reported in 2021 give Petit Manseng as a cross of Savagnin and an unknown variety, and the Oxford Companion says Savagnin may well be its parent. DNA alone cannot say which way a parent and offspring tie runs, hence likely. The grapes[1].styles line names the Traminer family and nothing about Sauvignon Blanc, so it is left; the Savagnin grape fragment already carries the likely parent on its card.

targets.new: Savagnin is not Sauvignon Blanc: it belongs to the Traminer family, kin to Gewürztraminer, and DNA makes it a likely parent of Sauvignon Blanc and of Petit Manseng.

entries.topic: Roussanne row: no Marsanne in Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc
entries.claim: The Régionale Roussanne row (INTRO_GRAPES) lists its wines as White Rhône blends: Hermitage, Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc (with Marsanne).
entries.finding: The Châteauneuf-du-Pape specification (homologated by decree no. 2011-1567, as published by the appellation's own federation) lists eighteen varieties: Bourboulenc, Brun Argenté (Vaccarèse), Cinsaut, Clairette, Clairette Rose, Counoise, Grenache Blanc, Grenache Gris, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Muscardin, Picardan, Piquepoul Blanc, Gris and Noir, Roussanne, Syrah and Terret Noir. Marsanne is not among them. White Hermitage is Marsanne and Roussanne. The row's reg string, N. Rhône blanc (with Marsanne), Châteauneuf blanc, Savoie, already ties Marsanne to the northern Rhône only, so it is left; Hermitage and Savoie stay where they are.

entries.topic: Muscadet lines that still hold: the grape implied, the 1709 replanting
entries.claim: The Loire record says the grape is implied by the appellation (Muscadet is Melon), its exam and trap lines match Muscadet to Melon de Bourgogne, and the stem of i-r0p7056l says a hard winter in 1709 killed most of the vineyard around Nantes and growers replanted with a hardy Burgundian white.
entries.finding: Melon B is the principal grape of every Muscadet appellation and the only grape of the three named ones; the plain appellation's accessory Chardonnay, at most 10 per cent of a holding's plantings, does not change which grape the name implies. The specification's own link to origin tells the 1709 replanting as the stem does.
